To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a genetically defined subpopulation of GABAAergic neurons in the lateral subdivision (CEl) of the central amygalda (Ce) gate conditioned fear by inhibiting the medial subdivision (CEm) of the central amgydala.
a specific subpopulation of neurons in CEl inhibits output neurons in CEm, and that this subpopulation is necessary for normal expression of Pavlovian conditioned freezing behaviour.

a subpopulation of PKC-Δ neurons in the lateral subdivision (CEl) of the central amygadala (CE) gate the level of conditioned fear by controlling the activity of neurons in the medial subdivision (CEm).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the function of the different types of neurons within the amygdala, which is a key brain structure for fear and anxiety.
the role of different amygalda nuclei (neuro-anatomical subdivisions) and their heterogeneous neuronal subtypes in processing Pavlovin conditioned fear.
the role of different amydgala nuclei (neural circuits) in processing Pavlonian conditioned fear, which is a form of learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PKC-Δ+ cells in the CEl are a subpopulation of neurons that are part of a microcircuit that controls the expression of conditioned fear.
the PKCδ+ neurons are part of a microcircuit that controls conditioned fear.
the lateral subdivision of central amygdala is an inhibitory micro-circuit that gates the output of the medial subdivision to control the level and duration of fear expression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CEl microcircuit is a gate that determines whether the CEm output neurons are activated.
a specific subpopulation of GABergic cells in the CEl, which are inhibited by the CS, gate the output to the CEm.
the CEm-CEl circuitry is a key site for controlling the strength of Pavlovian fear responses, with CEl inhibiting CEm output and thereby regulating the strength of the fear response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
genetically defined neuronal populations can be used to dissect the functional organization of complex microcircuits, and to understand their role in behaviour.
a subpopulation of CEl neurons, which are activated by the conditioned stimulus (CS), inhibit the downstream CEm neurons that drive the conditioned response.

genetically defined neuronal subpopulations can be functionally mapped by combining circuit-mapping techniques in slices with cell-specific viral tracing and in vivo electrophysiology, thereby providing a framework for the systematic genetic dissection of the functional organization of neuronal networks.
